notes.h: Finance needed to buy a home (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The amount a buyer must borrow is the purchase price minus the deposit, plus the other costs of buying.
points: Factors that determine the amount required: the purchase price, the size and location of the house, and the buyer's savings.
Additional costs of buying include solicitor's fees, stamp duty, the valuation and survey carried out for the lender, and any fitting-out costs.
A deposit is the buyer's own money paid towards the purchase price; the lender supplies the balance as a mortgage.
Sources of finance: the buyer's savings, a mortgage from a bank, building society or other lending institution, a credit union loan, or help from parents or family.
A mortgage is a loan secured on the house itself, so the lender can repossess the property if repayments are not made.

notes.h: Conditions attached to mortgage approval (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A lending institution assesses whether the applicant can repay the loan and whether the property is a suitable security for it.
points: Borrowing limit: the loan is capped at a set multiple of the applicant's gross income.
Loan-to-value limit: the loan cannot exceed a set share of the property's value, so the buyer must provide the balance as a deposit.
Secure employment: the applicant must be in stable work so that repayments can be met over the term.
Proof of income: payslips, a P60 and bank statements show the lender what the applicant earns.
Good credit history: evidence of steady saving and reasonable spending, with no record of missed repayments.
Term of the loan: repayments are spread over a long period, but an older applicant is usually offered a shorter term so the loan ends before retirement.
Property condition: the lender surveys the house, and it must be in good condition before the loan is released.

notes.b: A mortgage protection policy is a life assurance policy that protects the lender's loan and the borrower's family if the borrower dies during the term.
points: The policy pays off the outstanding mortgage balance if the borrower dies during the term of the loan.
Without cover, the remaining debt would fall on the borrower's family, who could be forced to sell the home.
Annuity and pension-linked mortgages require a mortgage protection policy to be taken out with the loan.
An endowment mortgage does not need a separate protection policy, because its life assurance policy already covers the loan.
Annuity (repayment) mortgage: each repayment pays part of the interest and part of the capital borrowed, so the amount owed falls over time. It is the most common type.
Endowment mortgage: the borrower pays interest on the loan and a premium on a life assurance policy designed to repay the loan when it matures, though the policy yield may not fully cover the loan.

Pension-linked mortgage: interest is paid on the loan and a sum is paid into a pension scheme, and the loan is repaid from the pension fund on retirement; popular with self-employed people because of tax relief on pension contributions.
Tracker mortgage: the interest rate follows a published benchmark rate, usually the European Central Bank rate, plus a fixed margin.
Interest-only mortgage: the borrower pays only the interest for a period, and the capital is still owed at the end of that period.
Current account (offset) mortgage: savings held in a linked current account reduce the balance on which interest is charged.

notes.h: Interest rates and repayments (Higher Level only)
points: A fixed rate stays the same for a set number of years, so repayments are constant during that period and protected from rises.
A variable rate moves with market interest rates, so repayments rise when rates rise and fall when rates fall.
A combination mortgage divides the loan between a fixed portion and a variable portion.
A fixed rate is usually higher than the variable rate at the start, because the lender takes on the risk of rate changes.
A shorter loan term means higher repayments but less interest paid in total.
Hire purchase is a way of buying goods such as furniture or appliances by paying in instalments.
The buyer does not own the goods until the final instalment is paid.
Hire purchase agreements are governed by the Consumer Credit Act 1995, as amended.
The annual percentage rate of charge must be disclosed to the consumer before the agreement is signed.

keyTerms.definition: The part of the purchase price paid by the buyer from their own funds, with the lender providing the rest.
A loan to buy property, secured on the property, which the lender can repossess if repayments are not made.
A life assurance policy that pays off the outstanding mortgage if the borrower dies during the loan term.
A borrower's total income before tax and deductions, used by lenders to set the maximum loan.
A repayment mortgage in which each repayment covers interest and part of the capital, so the debt reduces over the term.
A mortgage in which the borrower pays interest on the loan and a premium on a life assurance policy that is intended to repay the loan at maturity.
A mortgage whose interest rate moves in line with a published benchmark rate, plus a fixed margin.
An interest rate that changes with market rates, so the borrower's repayments can rise or fall.
A credit agreement in which goods are paid for in instalments, with ownership passing only after the final payment.
The total yearly cost of credit, expressed as a percentage, which must be disclosed to the borrower.

questions.prompt: Explain what a tracker mortgage is and how its repayments change over the loan term.
questions.model: A tracker mortgage has an interest rate that follows a published benchmark rate, usually the European Central Bank rate, plus a fixed margin. When the benchmark rate rises, the interest rate and repayments rise; when it falls, they fall. The repayments therefore vary over the term, and the borrower carries the risk of rate increases.

questions.prompt: Discuss the conditions a lending institution is likely to set before approving a mortgage, and explain the purpose of a mortgage protection policy.
questions.model: Borrowing limit: the loan is set as a multiple of gross income. Loan-to-value: the loan is limited to a share of the property's value, so the buyer must provide a deposit. Secure employment and proof of income: payslips and a P60 show the applicant can meet repayments. Good credit history and regular saving show sound financial management. Term of the loan: long repayment periods, with shorter terms for older applicants. Property condition: the house is surveyed and must be in good condition as security. Mortgage protection policy: a life assurance policy that pays off the outstanding balance if the borrower dies during the term, so that the family is not left with the debt and the lender is repaid. It is required with annuity and pension-linked mortgages, while an endowment mortgage's life policy serves the same purpose.
